summary: This experimental RFC specifies the Directional Airtime link metric for OLSRv2, a routing protocol for wireless mesh networks. It estimates link quality in each direction, using packet sequence numbers, so routing can prefer links that use radio time efficiently.

eli5.summary: Some wireless links waste more radio time than others. This gives a way to score each direction of a link so routers pick the faster paths.

questions: what is the directional airtime metric
why do wireless mesh networks need link metrics
how does dat metric measure packet loss
subtitle: Directional Airtime metric for wireless routing to prefer fast links over slow ones

tldr.problem: Hop-count routing in wireless mesh networks ignores link quality, causing routes to use slow or unreliable links that waste airtime, degrading network performance.
tldr.mechanism: The Directional Airtime (DAT) metric measures each incoming link by tracking packet loss rate and link speed, producing a dimensionless cost value that routing can use to prefer faster, more reliable paths.
tldr.outcome: Routing decisions can now account for wireless link variability, improving throughput and reducing latency in community mesh networks using OLSRv2.

today: RFC 7779 remains Experimental. It is designed for wireless mesh networks using IEEE 802.11 and OLSRv2. The RFC notes that the metric is a baseline for comparison and invites further experiments to move it to Standards Track or improve it.

sections.title: Link Quality and Mesh Routing
sections.content:
OLSRv2 (Optimized Link State Routing Version 2) is a routing protocol for wireless mesh networks. Early versions of OLSR used a hop-count metric: routes were chosen to minimize the number of hops between source and destination. However, in wireless networks, not all hops are equal. A link with high packet loss or a slow data rate can be far more expensive than a longer route via faster, more reliable links.

This mismatch is especially problematic in community mesh networks where routers have heterogeneous wireless cards and are deployed in varied RF environments. The original OLSR.org implementation used an Estimated Transmission Count (ETX) metric as a workaround, but ETX does not account for link speed. The Directional Airtime metric specified here improves on ETX by incorporating both loss rate and link speed into a single cost value.
sections.eli5: When a mesh router picks a path, using hop count is like choosing the fewest number of streets to walk without checking if they are clear. A smarter router looks at each link's quality and speed to find the fastest actual route.

sections.title: From Hop Count to Directional Metrics
sections.content:
OLSRv2 defined a pluggable architecture where each link gets a metric value—a cost assigned by some external mechanism. The Directional Airtime metric specifies how to calculate this cost for each incoming link to a neighbor, measuring only the incoming direction. It differs from earlier metrics like ETX and ETT (Estimated Travel Time) in three ways:

First, it is directional: it measures only the incoming link cost, not the combined cost of sending and receiving. This aligns with OLSRv2's design and avoids needing bidirectional signaling. Second, it incorporates link speed—a 100 Mbit/s link is cheaper per bit than a 1 Mbit/s link, even with equal loss. Third, it measures loss locally without waiting for acknowledgments, reducing measurement delay.
sections.eli5: The metric looks only at traffic coming in one direction, and it counts both how many packets are lost and how fast the link carries data. A fast reliable link gets a low cost.

sections.title: How Directional Airtime is Calculated
sections.content:
The metric processes packet arrivals to estimate two things: the packet loss rate and the link speed (which comes from an external source such as the operating system or a separate measurement process). Loss is tracked using two fixed-length queues, one for packets received and one for the total packets expected based on sequence numbers. Every DAT_REFRESH_INTERVAL seconds (default 1 second), the metric recalculates the link cost.

The calculation is: cost = (2^24 / 8) × (loss_rate) / (bitrate / 1000), where loss_rate is clamped to at most 7 out of 8 packets (87.5%). This produces a dimensionless cost: a link with 50% loss at 10 Mbit/s has the same cost as a link with 25% loss at 20 Mbit/s, because both waste the same airtime per successful packet. The metric handles link timeouts by scaling down received packets when the neighbor goes silent, detecting complete link loss.
sections.eli5: The router watches arriving packets and their sequence numbers to count how many were lost. It divides the loss rate by the link speed to get the true cost to the network—how much radio time is wasted per bit that gets through.

sections.title: Measurement and Implementation
sections.content:
The metric works with or without packet sequence numbers. When sequence numbers are present (the preferred way), the router counts gaps to directly estimate loss. Without them, the metric falls back to detecting loss by HELLO message timeouts, which is slower but still functional. The metric requires knowing the unicast bitrate for each neighbor; this comes from external measurement or configuration, possibly via a tool like DLEP (Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol).

Implementation adds several data structures to the routing information base: two queues per link for loss tracking, a packet timeout timer, and storage for sequence numbers and HELLO intervals. The queues smooth loss estimates over a configurable window (default 64 intervals) to avoid flickering metric values. A hysteresis filter can further stabilize the metric when link speed or loss varies.
sections.eli5: To measure loss, the router looks at packet sequence numbers in routing messages. If it expects packet 10 but gets packet 12, packet 11 was lost. The router keeps a history of recent packets to avoid false alarms from timing jitter.

sections.title: Vulnerabilities and Safeguards
sections.content:
Because metric values directly influence which routes the network uses, an attacker can disrupt routing by advertising false metrics. An attacker could advertise an artificially low metric to attract traffic, then drop the packets for a denial-of-service attack, or use the concentrated traffic for eavesdropping. Defending against this requires validating the authenticity of routing messages using MANET security mechanisms such as ICV (Integrity Check Value) and timestamp TLVs defined in RFC 7182 and 7183.

A limitation is that standard MANET security signs the routing messages but not the packet sequence numbers in the RFC 5444 packet header. An attacker can forge sequence numbers to manipulate loss estimates, but validating the overall routing message still prevents injection of entirely spoofed routes.
sections.eli5: An attacker could lie about link quality to trick the network into routing traffic through a compromised node. The solution is to sign routing messages so routers can verify they came from the real neighbor.
